newsitem.title: UK: British carriers await lifting of Nigerian ban.
newsitem.headline: British carriers await lifting of Nigerian ban.

text.p: British carriers are still awaiting the lifting of the Nigerian ban on all British-registered flights into the country, imposed on May 16, industry sources said.
A UK Department of Transport spokeswoman said it is trying to send inspectors to Nigeria to inspect Nigerian aircraft that would be used on the UK route.
A British Airways spokesman said that the situation is unchanged, with the ban on all British carriers still firmly in place.
"Talks are continuing between the British and Nigerian governments but it is purely a governmental matter, we are not involved in the talks," the BA official said.
"We hope they come to a settlement soon so we can resume our flights as soon as possible," he added.
However, the British Civil Aviation Authority's inspection team were being denied visas by the Nigerian authorities.
Attempts are being made to find a third country where the inspection could take place or somewhere in the UK that is not near any population centres, she said.
Once the inspection takes place, we are hoping the situation can be resolved, she added.

DHL's area manager for West Africa, Edward Bellord, told Reuters by telephone that the ban had reduced capacity on the Lagos-London route by two wide-body aircraft a day. The Nigeria market is DHL's second largest after South Africa in Africa.
He said there is no problem for the express operator on the outbound services ex-Nigeria to Europe, as there is still plenty of capacity.
Southbound uplift from Europe is where the problem lies. The UK business accounts for approximately 25 percent of inbound Nigerian air express.
DHL estimates that it holds a 60 to 65 percent share of the Nigerian outbound express market.
The express operator is using carriers such as Lufthansa, via Frankfurt and Sabena through DHL's European hub in Brussels and KLM via Amsterdam.
DHL is also using Air Afrique into Abidjan and transhipping on to Lagos, which can result in delays of 24-hours, he added. DHL International holds a three percent share in Air Afrique.
The express company is also looking into the possibility of operating dedicated charters between Lagos its West Africa hub in Abidjan.
DHL is in talks with Air Afrique and other African carriers and expects to make a final decision on the charter operation and type of aircraft to be used in the next five days.
This would only be to supplement uplift when DHL could not get enough capacity from the other carriers flying into Nigeria, he stressed.
Bellord said that because DHL's network in West Africa is wholly owned and controlled by DHL, the company has advantages over its competitors in these situations.
DHL had not lost any business into Nigeria, although cargo is subject to delays, he added.

Under its usual schedule BA operates a daily B747 flight to Lagos and a three-times-weekly DC-10 service to Kano which travels on to Accra in Ghana. Kano has been by-passed, although the service to Accra continues.

The Nigerian government imposed the ban following the British government's move to bar Nigerian flights two months previously on safety grounds. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+44 171 542--5017
